title: Superconducting $T_\mathrm{c}$ up to 20.6 K in bulk YSi$_2$ and YSi$_2$/Si superlattices due to chemical flattening
authors: Ding-qing Li, Chong Tian, Juan Du, Jun-jie Shi, Pei-song He, Deng-hui Xu, Hong-xia Zhong, Yao-hui Zhu
abstract: Currently, the fundamental building blocks of leading quantum computers are Josephson junctions, whose core is usually the superconducting Al on Si wafers. However, the transition temperature $T_\mathrm{c}$ of bulk Al ($\sim1.1$ K) is below the boiling point of liquid helium ($\sim4.2$ K), which is one of the challenges to its widespread application. Here, we propose a Si-matched AlB$_2$-type superconductor YSi$_2$ as a promising alternative to Al. The solution of anisotropic (isotropic) Migdal-Eliashberg equation without (with) anharmonicity gives $T_\mathrm{c}\sim20.6$ K ($17.2$ K), which is at the highest level in silicides. Its excellent superconductivity can be attributed mainly to the Si honeycombs, which become plane here due to the 'chemical flattening' effects of the Y atoms instead of being buckled in most silicides. We tested its thermodynamical, kinetic, dynamical, and mechanical stability by first-principles calculations. Particularly, the negative elastic stiffness constant $C_{66}$ calculated by usual methods turns positive even without the zero-point energy once the Si honeycombs are compressed below a threshold. This strain can also make its calculated lattice constants agree with the experimental ones. We propose structures to realize this strain, i.e., YSi$_2$(0001)/Si(111) superlattices, which can also strengthen the overall stability of YSi$_2$ while maintaining its $T_\mathrm{c}$ above $7.0$ K.
summary: This paper proposes YSi2 as a high-temperature superconductor alternative to Al for quantum computing. Using first-principles calculations, the authors predict a $T_c$ of 20.6 K, attributing this enhancement to structural changes called 'chemical flattening.' They further propose strain engineering via superlattices to maximize stability and superconducting performance.
main_problem: To develop high-temperature superconducting materials suitable for quantum computing applications, overcoming the low critical temperature ($T_c$) of standard Al/Si junctions.
main_result: The material YSi2 exhibits a predicted $T_c$ up to 20.6 K due to 'chemical flattening' effects in its Si honeycombs; superlattices are proposed to enhance stability and maintain high $T_c$.
method: Theoretical calculations using first-principles methods, including solving the Migdal-Eliashberg equations (both isotropic and anisotropic) and performing extensive stability checks (thermodynamic, kinetic, mechanical).
model_or_system: The focus is on YSi2, an AlB2-type superconductor proposed as a replacement for Al. The study models both bulk structures and engineered superlattices like YSi2(0001)/Si(111) to control strain.
key_observables: $T_c$, elastic stiffness constant ($C_{66}$), formation energy ($\Delta E$), lattice constants ($a, c$).
important_parameters: Superconducting transition temperature (up to 20.6 K); compressive strain; anharmonicity effects.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on DFT calculations and approximations within the Migdal-Eliashberg theory framework; some results are based on theoretical predictions of stability under strain.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate crystal structures (bulk vs. superlattice), AIMD energy fluctuations showing kinetic stability, and phonon spectra used for calculating superconducting parameters.
paper_structure: The work proceeds by first identifying the problem (low $T_c$ of Al), proposing YSi2 as a solution, then using multiple theoretical tools (ME equations, stability analysis) to calculate high $T_c$, and finally engineering superlattices to realize necessary strain states.
why_interesting: While focused on superconductivity rather than quantum information directly, the work involves advanced many-body calculations (Migdal-Eliashberg theory) and material design principles crucial for realizing superconducting components in quantum devices.

FIG. 4. The variation of c with a. In the strainless state, a = 4.07 ˚A and c = 3.89 ˚A are determined by the PBEsol functional. For the same a = 4.07 ˚A, the SCAN functional yields c = 3.98 ˚A, which is larger than the PBEsol one by 2.3%. When a was compressed below a critical value ∼3.98 ˚A, C66 would turn positive even without the ZPE correction. The red square denotes the experimental lattice constants, i.e., a = 3.842 ˚A and c = 4.14 ˚A. The experimental c is larger than the corresponding PBEsol result by only 1.5%, and almost identical to that given by the SCAN functional.
